strengths: The per-orientation analysis reveals structured generalization patterns that average accuracy obscures. These findings have an identifiable audience among researchers studying visual robustness, learned invariance, and neural representations.

The experimental design systematically varies object category, training orientations, and the proportion of fully seen instances while holding the total number of identities and training images constant. Five randomized repetitions and reported variability strengthen the descriptive evidence.

Experiments with DenseNet, CORnet-S, and ViT, alongside pretraining, augmentation, and reduced-data controls, provide useful evidence that the observed patterns extend beyond one architecture or training configuration. The narrower coverage of the alternative architectures is disclosed.

The geometric decomposition into small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related components is interpretable and achieves strong reported fits. The manuscript is broadly understandable, with informative visualizations, explicit analytical definitions, and links to code and data.
weaknesses: Necessary: The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Figures 5b–c establish associations between activation statistics and accuracy, but do not establish that invariance transfers directionally from fully seen to partially seen instances through shared features. Shared image geometry and joint training could produce these associations. Sections 3.3–4 should consistently present dissemination as a hypothesis supported by correlations, or provide targeted interventions that distinguish it from alternatives. The conclusion that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs also requires narrower wording.

Necessary: Predictive validity is not established independently of fitting. Section 2.4 optimizes the logistic parameters directly against network accuracy using Pearson correlation, and Section 3.2 reports that same statistic without specifying a held-out evaluation. These results support descriptive goodness of fit. Claims of prediction from the seed orientations require an explicit fitting/evaluation separation, such as held-out experiments or orientation regions; alternatively, describe the model as a retrospective characterization.

Necessary: The definition of generalizable orientations needs clarification and validation. Section 2.5 thresholds the model at 10% of its maximum, although Equation 4 sums four logistic outputs and fits only correlation, which does not calibrate the prediction's offset or scale to accuracy. An additive offset preserves Pearson correlation but changes this partition. Figure S9c's approximately 1.8–2.4 score range also needs reconciliation with the stated rule. Specify any omitted normalization and demonstrate partition stability, because Figures 5 and S8 depend on this definition.

Necessary: The invariance statistic does not directly establish invariance across individual views. Equations 5–7 compare activation averages over orientation sets; equal averages can conceal substantial variation within either set. Requiring both averages to exceed the 95th-percentile activity threshold also excludes neuron–instance pairs whose responses disappear in one set. Validate the interpretation using variation across individual orientations and report sensitivity to the threshold and the fraction of retained pairs, or restrict the claim to similarity of regional mean activations.

Necessary scope correction: Comparing the default dataset with half as much data does not establish the data-saturated, 'most favorable' regime asserted in Section 2.1. Similarly, Figure 4a includes relatively flat or decreasing trends for some seed/category combinations. Qualify the saturation claim and describe the diversity effect with its observed exceptions.

Optional improvements: Enlarge the dense labels in Figures 4 and S5–S8 and report numerical, stratified summaries of the Figure 5 associations. Extensions to natural images or additional learning objectives would broaden applicability.
